```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)

library(AlphaSimR)
```

## Introduction

`vignette("traits")` describes the model `AlphaSimR` uses to turn
genotypes into genetic values, and how the `addTrait` functions sample and
scale the effects. This article is the practical companion. It shows how
to inspect a trait once it exists, how to control the distribution of its
effects, how to set effects by hand, how to ask for dominance in terms
of variances rather than dominance degrees, and how to record traits
that are not continuous, such as scores and counts.

```{r}
set.seed(1918)

founderPop = quickHaplo(nInd = 500, nChr = 5, segSites = 200)

SP = SimParam$new(founderPop)
```
```{r include=FALSE}
SP$nThreads = 1L
```

## Inspecting a trait

Every trait is stored in `SP$traits` as an object whose class names its
type, holding the positions of its QTL, their effects and the trait's
intercept:

```{r}
SP$addTraitA(nQtlPerChr = 100, name = "Normal")

trait = SP$traits[[1]]
class(trait)[1]
trait@intercept
head(trait@addEff)
head(getQtlMap(trait = 1, simParam = SP))
```

The effects are on the scale of the scaled additive dosage, so for a
diploid each copy of the "1" allele adds `addEff` to the genetic value.

## The distribution of effects

By default additive effects are sampled from a normal distribution. With
`gamma = TRUE` they are sampled from a gamma distribution with the given
`shape`, and given a random sign. A small shape gives a few loci with
large effects and many with very small ones, which is closer to what
mapping studies report for many traits [@hayes2001Distribution].

```{r}
SP$addTraitA(nQtlPerChr = 100, gamma = TRUE, shape = 0.3,
             name = "Gamma")

pop = newPop(founderPop, simParam = SP)
```

Both traits were scaled to the same additive variance, but the variance
is spread over the loci very differently. The genic variance a locus
contributes is $2p(1-p)a^2$ for a diploid, so the share contributed by
the largest loci can be calculated directly:

```{r}
topShare = function(t, top = 0.05){
  a = SP$traits[[t]]@addEff
  p = colMeans(pullQtlGeno(pop, trait = t, simParam = SP)) / 2
  v = sort(2 * p * (1 - p) * a^2, decreasing = TRUE)
  sum(v[seq_len(ceiling(top * length(v)))]) / sum(v)
}

round(c(Normal = topShare(1), Gamma = topShare(2)), 3)
```

```{r fig.width=7, fig.height=3.5}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
hist(SP$traits[[1]]@addEff, breaks = 40, main = "Normal",
     xlab = "Additive effect")
hist(SP$traits[[2]]@addEff, breaks = 40, main = "Gamma, shape 0.3",
     xlab = "Additive effect")
```

With normal effects, the largest 5% of QTL contribute about a quarter of
the genic variance; with gamma effects of shape 0.3, about two thirds.
The distinction matters for anything that depends on individual loci:
genomic prediction, the speed at which selection fixes alleles, and how
long variance lasts under selection. A trait with a few large QTL loses
its variance in steps, as each one is fixed.

## Setting effects yourself

### From names and effects

When the effects should come from somewhere else, such as a mapping
study, `importTrait` adds a trait from the names of its QTL and their
effects. The QTL must be segregating sites of the founder population.
The example builds a mixture: five loci of large effect among many of
small effect.

```{r}
SPmix = SimParam$new(founderPop)
```
```{r include=FALSE}
SPmix$nThreads = 1L
```
```{r}
siteNames = getGenMap(SPmix)$id
qtl = sample(siteNames, 200)
effects = c(rnorm(5, sd = 1), rnorm(195, sd = 0.05))

SPmix$importTrait(markerNames = qtl, addEff = effects, name = "Mixture")
```

`importTrait` uses the effects exactly as given, so the founder variance
is whatever they imply. `rescaleTraits` then rescales every trait to a
requested mean and variance in the founder population, keeping the
relative sizes of the effects:

```{r}
summarize = function(x, simParam){
  round(c(mean = unname(meanG(x)[1]),
          varA = varA(x, simParam = simParam)[1, 1],
          genicVarA = unname(genicVarA(x, simParam = simParam)[1])), 3)
}

popMix = newPop(founderPop, simParam = SPmix)
summarize(popMix, SPmix)

SPmix$rescaleTraits(mean = 10, var = 2)
popMix = resetPop(popMix, simParam = SPmix)
summarize(popMix, SPmix)
```

Existing populations keep their old genetic values until `resetPop`
recalculates them.

### Rescaling to a later population

`rescaleTraits` scales against `SP$founderPop`, which is the founder
population the `SimParam` was created with. Replacing it makes the
traits scale against another population instead, which is the intended
way to put traits on a standard scale after a burn-in: for example, mean
0 and additive variance 1 in the population where the comparison of
breeding programs begins.

This is for advanced use, because it breaks every existing population.
Their genetic values, phenotypes and estimated breeding values were
computed on the old scale. `resetPop` must be run on any population that
is kept: it recalculates the genetic values, but it clears the
phenotypes and estimated breeding values, so they have to be generated
again. Anything else computed before the change, such as a fitted
genomic or pedigree model, a stored summary or a selection index, is on
the old scale and must be recomputed too. The residual variances are
not rescaled with the traits, so they must be reset as well.

```{r}
# Five generations of selection on genetic values, since this trait has
# no error variance and so no phenotypes
burnIn = popMix
for(i in 1:5){
  burnIn = selectCross(burnIn, nInd = 50, nCrosses = 250, nProgeny = 2,
                       use = "gv", simParam = SPmix)
}
summarize(burnIn, SPmix)

# Frequencies of the five loci of largest effect, before and after
largeQtl = order(abs(SPmix$traits[[1]]@addEff), decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]
round(rbind(
  founders = colMeans(pullQtlGeno(popMix, simParam = SPmix))[largeQtl] / 2,
  burnIn = colMeans(pullQtlGeno(burnIn, simParam = SPmix))[largeQtl] / 2
), 2)

# Rescale against the burned-in population, reset the residual
# variance, then recalculate genetic values and phenotypes
SPmix$founderPop = burnIn
SPmix$rescaleTraits(mean = 0, var = 1)
SPmix$setVarE(h2 = 0.3)
burnIn = resetPop(burnIn, simParam = SPmix)
burnIn = setPheno(burnIn, simParam = SPmix)
summarize(burnIn, SPmix)
varP(burnIn)
```

Five generations of strong selection removed most of the additive
variance, in two ways. Allele frequencies changed: four of the five loci
of large effect were fixed and the fifth nearly so, which shows as the
fall in genic variance, the variance the population would have at its
allele frequencies in linkage equilibrium. Selection also created
negative linkage disequilibrium between the loci that still segregate,
which is the Bulmer effect [@bulmer1971Effect]: the additive variance is
below the genic variance because favorable alleles at one locus have
come to be paired with unfavorable alleles at others. The
[Quantitative Genetics](QuanGen.html) article describes this
partition in more detail.

Rescaling sets the additive variance, disequilibrium included, to the
requested value. The disequilibrium is not permanent: if selection
stops, recombination breaks it down, fastest between unlinked loci, and
the additive variance rises toward the genic variance, above the
requested value. Three generations of random mating show it:

```{r}
relaxed = burnIn
for(i in 1:3){
  relaxed = randCross(relaxed, nCrosses = 500, simParam = SPmix)
}
summarize(relaxed, SPmix)
```

The additive variance rose from 1 to about 1.6, nearly the genic
variance, while the genic variance itself hardly changed. Rescaling
against a population still in strong disequilibrium therefore gives a
scale whose additive variance will not stay at the requested value. Bear
that in mind when choosing the reference population and the target
variance; rescaling after a few generations of random mating, once the
disequilibrium has largely decayed, avoids the drift.

`setVarE(h2 = 0.3)` sets the residual variance from the rescaled
additive variance, so that the heritability in the reference population
is the requested 0.3. Without it, the residual variance would keep its
old value on the old scale, or here, since this trait had none, there
would be no phenotypes at all.

`importTrait` also takes dominance effects with `domEff`, and
additive-by-additive epistasis with `epiPairs` and `epiEff`; the
[Importing Data](ImportingData.html) article has an example.

### Editing an existing trait

Because a trait is an ordinary S4 object, an existing trait can be
copied, changed and added with `manAddTrait`. Here the five loci of
largest effect in the normal trait are made ten times larger, and the
result is added to a new `SimParam` built from the same founders. Traits
can only be added before any population is created, which is why a new
`SimParam` is used rather than `SP`:

```{r}
edited = SP$traits[[1]]
largest = order(abs(edited@addEff), decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]
edited@addEff[largest] = edited@addEff[largest] * 10
edited@name = "Edited"

SPedit = SimParam$new(founderPop)
```
```{r include=FALSE}
SPedit$nThreads = 1L
```
```{r}
SPedit$manAddTrait(edited)
SPedit$traitNames
```

The edited trait is not rescaled, so its mean and variance in the founders
are whatever the new effects imply. `manAddTrait` accepts any object
descended from `LociMap`, so a trait can also be built from scratch with
`new()`, but that requires knowing the slots of the trait classes, and
`importTrait` is usually easier.

## Dominance by variance

`addTraitAD` describes dominance by the distribution of dominance degrees,
which has a clear meaning at one locus but leaves the resulting dominance
variance and inbreeding depression to be discovered. `altAddTraitAD`
works the other way round: it takes the additive variance, the dominance
variance `varD` and the inbreeding depression `inbrDepr` wanted in the
founders, and searches for a mean and variance of dominance degrees that
achieve them, within the limits `limMeanDD` and `limVarDD`.

```{r}
SPad = SimParam$new(founderPop)
```
```{r include=FALSE}
SPad$nThreads = 1L
```
```{r}
SPad$altAddTraitAD(nQtlPerChr = 100, mean = 0, varA = 1, varD = 0.2,
                   inbrDepr = 1)
```

The summary reports what was achieved. The mean and additive variance
are always exact; the dominance variance and inbreeding depression are
met only as closely as the limits on the dominance degrees allow, so the
summary is worth reading. Inbreeding depression here is the difference in
mean between the founders and a fully inbred population with the same
allele frequencies. Doubled haploids of the founders are such a
population:

```{r}
popAD = newPop(founderPop, simParam = SPad)
dhAD = makeDH(popAD, simParam = SPad)

c(varD = varD(popAD, simParam = SPad)[1, 1],
  inbreedingDepression = unname(meanG(popAD) - meanG(dhAD)))
```

The dominance variance matches the request, and the drop in mean from the
founders to their doubled haploids is close to the requested inbreeding
depression of 1. It is not exact, because one doubled haploid per founder
is a finite sample whose allele frequencies differ slightly from the
founders'.

## Traits that are not continuous

Phenotypes in `AlphaSimR` are continuous, but many traits are recorded as
scores, categories or counts. The usual way to simulate them is a
threshold or link model: the continuous phenotype is a latent value, and
what is recorded is a function of it [@dempster1950Heritability]. Three functions apply such
transformations to a matrix or vector of values:

- `asCategorical` cuts the latent scale into ordered categories, either
  at given `threshold`s or so that proportions `p` fall in each category;
- `asLogNormal` returns `exp(x)`, optionally shifted on the log scale;
- `asPoisson` draws counts with mean `exp(x)`, also optionally shifted.

```{r}
SPcat = SimParam$new(founderPop)
```
```{r include=FALSE}
SPcat$nThreads = 1L
```
```{r}
SPcat$addTraitA(nQtlPerChr = 100)
SPcat$setVarE(h2 = 0.5)
popCat = newPop(founderPop, simParam = SPcat)

# Three categories in proportions 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3 of a normal latent
# scale with the phenotypic mean and variance
latent = pheno(popCat)[, 1]
score = asCategorical(latent, p = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.3),
                      mean = 0, var = varP(popCat)[1, 1])
prop.table(table(score))
```

The thresholds come from a normal distribution with the given `mean`
and `var`, so the realized proportions are close to `p` but not exact.

### Recording the transformed trait automatically

Applying the transformation by hand works for one population. To have
every phenotype in the simulation recorded on the new scale, set
`SP$finalizePheno`, a function applied to every new matrix of phenotypes,
including those from later calls to `setPheno`:

```{r}
SPcat$finalizePheno = function(pheno, pop, simParam, ...){
  pheno[, 1] = asCategorical(pheno[, 1], p = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.3),
                             mean = 0, var = 2)
  pheno
}

popScored = setPheno(popCat, simParam = SPcat)
table(pheno(popScored)[, 1])
```

The function receives the phenotype matrix, the population and the
`SimParam`, and must return a matrix with the same rows and columns. The
latent variance is written as 2 here, the phenotypic variance in the
founders for a trait with a genetic variance of 1 and a heritability of
0.5. The thresholds then stay fixed as the population changes under
selection, which is the right model for a fixed recording scale, such as
a score from 1 to 3.

### Selecting on a score

A score carries less information than the latent value it was cut from,
so selection on it achieves less. Many individuals share a score, and
ties are broken by order, so a small random value is added to break them
at random instead:

```{r}
nSel = 100
byLatent = selectInd(popCat, nInd = nSel, simParam = SPcat)
byScore = selectInd(popCat, nInd = nSel, simParam = SPcat,
                    use = function(pop, trait){
                      score + runif(length(score), 0, 1e-6)
                    })

round(c(latent = unname(meanG(byLatent) - meanG(popCat)),
        score = unname(meanG(byScore) - meanG(popCat))), 3)
```

Selecting on the three-category score gave a little under 80% of the
genetic superiority of selecting on the latent phenotype. In general,
the fewer the categories, the more is lost.

### Counts

`asPoisson` models counts through a log link. Applied to genetic values,
it gives counts whose expected value depends on the genotype; the shift
`meanLogShift` sets the average count:

```{r}
counts = asPoisson(gv(popCat)[, 1], meanLogShift = log(2))
c(mean = mean(counts), var = var(counts))
table(counts)
```

The mean count is above 2 because the genetic values vary on the log
scale: with a mean of 0 and a variance of 1, the average of
$2e^{x}$ is $2e^{1/2} \approx 3.3$. For the same reason the counts are
far more variable than Poisson counts with a single mean, which is the
overdispersion seen in real count data. A smaller genetic variance on the
log scale gives counts closer to Poisson.

## Changing every population as it is made

`SP$finalizePop` is the population-level counterpart of `finalizePheno`:
a function applied as the last step of creating any new population, with
the population as its first argument and the `SimParam` as its second. It
is a convenient place to attach data to every population, such as the
`misc` slots described in the [Misc](Misc.html) article. Because every
population then carries the same `misc` elements, they also survive
merging.

```{r}
SPcat$finalizePop = function(pop, simParam, ...){
  pop@misc$family = paste(pop@mother, pop@father, sep = "_")
  pop
}

progeny = randCross(popCat, nCrosses = 10, nProgeny = 3, simParam = SPcat)
head(progeny@misc$family)
```

`finalizePop` runs on every population the package creates, including
populations made inside other functions, so it should be quick and should
not assume anything about the population beyond its class. Setting it
back to `function(pop, ...) pop` turns it off.
